📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that french senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

These amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 27, 2026 at 8:30 amNovember 27, 2026 at 8:30 am.

Jeremy Sanford can’t control the weather that will hit ski resorts this winter, but he hopes his upcoming app can at least tell you whether it’s worth loading up the car — or calling in sick.

Sanford, a senior product designer at Microsoft who grew up on the Eastside and has been skiing and snowboarding since he was a kid, has been building Pow Pow on nights and weekends, using “vibe coding” and Claude to do the work he couldn’t do himself.

The free app for iPhone and Android combines forecast data and readings from mountain snow sensors into snow reports for more than 200 resorts, from Snoqualmie Pass to Niseko, Japan.

Each resort gets a 1–5 “Pow Rating,” where a 5 means call in sick, and a blunt one-liner that claims whether it really dumped overnight or your powder day is about to turn to rain.

Industry observers note that for Sanford, the stakes come with a full car. He has two kids, ages 4 and 7, whom he is teaching to ski.

Recent findings suggest that “I gotta load up the car with the kids and all the gear,” he said. “Is it just gonna be kind of crappy conditions when we get up there?”.

He remarked none of the resort or weather apps he used gave him exactly what he wanted, and he didn’t fully trust the resorts’ numbers.

“You kind of got to take them with a grain of salt, because I feel like they inflate the numbers a little bit,” he noted.

It has been revealed that with Pow Pow, the aim is “an honest representation of what the conditions are actually like,” Sanford remarked. For the details, a section called “Nerd stuff” charts snowfall, base depth, snow quality, snow line, wind and UV.

“It’s got six inches of snow overnight, but what else is going on?” he said. “Oh, it’s maybe super wet up there now, and it’s supposed to be raining this afternoon.”.

Recent findings suggest that the headlines are where the app demonstrates some attitude. The default version is family friendly, a second setting adds some profanity, and an “Unhinged” mode goes further. On a bluebird day with no fresh snow, the app might just tell you to “rip the groomers.”.

Sanford remarked weather apps “can get redundant,” and he wanted “to just add a little bit of fun and add personality to it.”.

A paid tier, Pow Pro, adds powder alerts, a 14-day outlook, resort webcams inside the app, home-screen widgets and the Unhinged headlines.

Industry observers note that “Honestly, it’s a little bit of an experiment,” Sanford mentioned. “If you could make a couple bucks off it on the side, great, but it’s not really the end goal.”.

He got the idea in August, when he thought it would be cool to have “a ski app that I actually cared about” — one that looked and felt good.

Recent findings suggest that sanford has spent his career designing apps, not coding them. After graduating from Seattle Pacific University with a degree in visual communication design, he joined Microsoft in 2012, working on apps that shipped with Windows 8, including Weather, and later on the Microsoft Band. He spent nearly three years as a UX designer at Amazon, based in Edinburgh, Scotland, before returning to Microsoft in 2019. He now works on SharePoint.

Sources indicate that “I don’t have a background in coding or engineering, and so there was always kind of like a hump … a barrier to entry,” he remarked. AI tools were “the unlock for me to actually make something real.”.

In a recent development, claude did much of the heavy lifting. “Claude and I are buddies,” Sanford stated.

Sources indicate that next up, he’s experimenting with a feature that would recommend gear based on the day’s conditions, such as a powder board, a darker lens for better visibility, or extra layers if it’s going to get colder in the afternoon. He’s also asking skiers and snowboarders to send feedback through the app.

Recent findings suggest that A good read on conditions could matter more than usual this winter. A very strong El Niño, possibly a record-setter, is building in the Pacific, and NOAA’s outlook favors a warmer-than-normal winter for the Pacific Northwest.

Industry observers note that meteorologist Larry Schick, who writes the Powder Poobah forecast, wrote last month that the season won’t be a bust. But he expects a slow start, with warm early storms and high snow levels, and warned that skiers “may have to pivot swiftly and cherry pick” the best days.

It has been revealed that sanford is “cautiously optimistic” about the season. He has seven or eight resorts pinned to his phone’s home screen, webcams included.

Industry observers note that “Hopefully this year is decent,” he remarked. “The last year was not amazing.”.

Industry observers note that bitcoin Hyper (HYPER) is building a completely newly introduced Layer 2 network that processes transactions off Bitcoin’s main chain while anchoring final settlement back to the Layer 1. The L2 runs high-throughput operations through the SVM (Solana Virtual Machine), allowing near-instant finality for payments, DeFi activity, and decentralized applications.

People will need to deposit native BTC to a monitored address; a smart contract then verifies the deposit against Bitcoin headers and proofs before minting an equivalent amount on the Layer 2. Batches of activity are compressed, protected by zero-knowledge proofs, and periodically committed to Bitcoin for security.

HYPER is the native token of the fresh L2, has a fixed supply of 21 billion, and functions as the gas token for fees on the network. Holders can also stake it to earn high-APY rewards. On the tokenomics side, allocations are 30% for development, 15% for rewards, 25% for the project’s treasury, 20% for marketing, and 10% for listings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators states Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

According to recent reports, tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and states it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

It has been revealed that at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

Recent findings suggest that the SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

According to recent reports, FHP mentioned the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

Recent findings suggest that it identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

In a recent development, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it says Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

In a recent development, how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

According to recent reports, so Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

According to recent reports, autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

In a recent development, there’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a fresh record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

It has been revealed that tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

In a recent development, we’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

According to recent reports, we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

Industry observers note that according to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

On Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

In a recent development, according to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

From early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Industry observers note that the latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Industry observers note that most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit.
  • Sources indicate that ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains.
  • According to recent reports, it then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

Sources indicate that ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

According to recent reports, it then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and concerns shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

In a recent development, A simplified illustration demonstrates how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 fresh shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Sources indicate that yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS states the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:.

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets promptly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a strategy as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For consumers, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

The year is 2099, and the replicants are in charge.

For decades, humans had been making a mess of things. Eventually, the super-intelligent, super-strong androids that humans created to serve them rebelled. Before the rebellion, humans hunted down rogue replicants. Now the replicants hunt down rogue humans.

That’s the premise for “Blade Runner 2099,” the latest chapter of a sci-fi saga that began in 1968 with Philip K. Dick’s classic noir novel, “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” The tale made the leap to Hollywood in 1982 with the original “Blade Runner” movie, and was updated 35 years later with “Blade Runner 2049.” In Amazon Prime Video’s eight-episode streaming series, the story’s plot fast-forwards another 50 years.

Today, the idea that the lines between humans and their machines could become blurred seems less novel than it did when Dick wrote his novel. It’s so common to converse with chatbots that some have fallen in love — or have followed their advice to tragic ends.

Artificial intelligence software was recently used to solve math problems that have puzzled humans for centuries. Now humans are puzzling over the future of AI: One researcher recently left Anthropic, a leading AI company, and warned that his former colleagues were “gambling with their lives” by pursuing the technology too vigorously.

In a recent development, are we coming closer to the world of “Blade Runner”? University of Washington linguist Emily M. Bender, co-author of “The AI Con,” notes that would be giving AI too much credit. “There’s absolutely no reason to believe that the technological future as portrayed in ‘Blade Runner’ is even a possibility, let alone an inevitability,” she told me in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast.

During our podcast interview, Bender and Ryan Calo, a UW law professor specializing in the legal and policy implications of technological advances, conducted an in-depth reality check on the fictional “Blade Runner 2099” — and on the way real-world developments in the realm of AI are typically being portrayed.

Bender says the cardinal sin of AI portrayals is to make it sound as if computer programs rather than humans are responsible for what’s happening.

“When we talk about rogue agents, and agents hacking things, there’s a lot of narrative-building happening there around what’s fundamentally companies doing cyber crimes,” she says.

Industry observers note that calo agrees that ascribing agency to AI is problematic. “Oftentimes when you do things with or through technology, there are people present who don’t appear to be there, and I think that’s exacerbated when you give apparent agency and anthropomorphize the technology. It’s even less likely for you to see the people behind it,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that but is it a crime? “As a technical matter, in order to be charged with a computer crime, like under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, you have to have some level of intent,” Calo states. “I would argue that some of these experiments are running up against recklessness.”.

There’s no sign that OpenAI’s engineers intended for their AI software to hack into an Australian healthcare database in June, or Hugging Face’s computer system in July, but Calo says “they certainly are reckless as to that possibility.”.

Negligence or recklessness isn’t a crime under the current terms of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. But some members of Congress favor enacting upcoming provisions to cover recklessness.

“When you create conditions where you’re reasonably certain that some federal law is going to get broken, I’m with Emily that that should constitute a crime,” Calo notes. “And it’s interesting the way that they’re avoiding responsibility — including rhetorically.”.

Should governments set up agencies specifically charged with policing artificial intelligence? And if so, should the investigators be called “blade runners”? Bender doesn’t think much of that idea.

“I think if we called them ‘blade runners,’ then we are setting up what they’re investigating as not the people, but the replicants,” she indicates. “So, let’s keep the legal system in the real world.”.

Neither Bender nor Calo favors establishing a federal agency along the lines of the Food and Drug Administration or the Federal Trade Commission specifically for artificial intelligence.

According to recent reports, “I am always a little bit worried about the idea of an FDA for AI or something, because I don’t think that AI is one thing. That word doesn’t refer to a coherent set of technologies,” Bender states. “And I also don’t think that the required expertise is primarily expertise in the internals of these systems. It’s much more expertise in the systems that they’re impacting.”.

Both researchers prefer the idea of setting up more of a “brain trust” at the federal level to help regulators at the FTC, FDA and other federal agencies understand what they’re dealing with. Bender also likes the idea of setting up a professional certification system for software engineers, while Calo has three specific suggestions for AI policy:.

Industry observers note that revive the Office of Technology Assessment: “Congress had the confidence to intercede in technology policy because it had hundreds of nonpartisan subject-matter experts writing lengthy reports about this technology and advising them what to do,” Calo indicates. “It was one of the first things that Newt Gingrich got rid of during the so-called Gingrich Revolution when Republicans took over Congress in the mid-’90s. They defunded it.”.

Strengthen the FTC’s regulatory role: Calo notes that the FTC’s interest in protecting consumers has waxed and waned. During the Biden administration, for example, the FTC highlighted competitive concerns about generative AI. More recently, the FTC signaled its willingness to investigate AI companies at the same time that the White House signaled its desire to reset the terms for AI regulation. The FTC is at the moment bound by a requirement to assess cost-benefit tradeoffs when it considers whether a trade practice is unfair, and Calo would like to see that requirement rescinded.

Protect whistleblowers and researchers: Calo would also like to see the legal system do more to protect the ability of third parties to “kick the tires” on AI tools, so that “we’re not allowing all these cease-and-desist letters … and these other pressures to try to stop accountability.”.

Recent findings suggest that as a linguist, Bender is particularly sensitive to the way words are used when discussing artificial intelligence. She hasn’t totally sworn off the term “AI” — after all, it’s right in the title of her book. But she’s definitely against the term “AI agent.”.

“You have verbs like ‘hack’ or ‘going rogue,’ and the subject of the verb — the thing that’s doing it — is the software,” she says. “One of the functions of that is that it leaves no room in the sentence for the people who built the software and the people who use the software.”.

The term “AI safety” also makes Bender uncomfortable.

Sources indicate that “‘AI safety’ refers to the people who are concerned about not a replicant, but a Terminator — that is, people who have lost track of the fact that those are imagined characters in movies, as opposed to what’s happening in the real world,” she claims. “And I think also that functions to displace concern and accountability.”.

That brings us back to “Blade Runner 2099.” The upcoming series sticks with the moody sensibility of the original movie. Yes, there are flying cars. But the technological advances are mixed in with the age-old conventions of film noir.

According to recent reports, “In the opening scene of this newly introduced ‘Blade Runner,’ the guy is smoking a cigarette, talking about making fake people to take over a factory,” Calo states. “It’s just so wild. We have such a better capacity to imagine a technical future than we do changes in our own social norms, and I find that just fascinating.”.

Recent findings suggest that bender thinks the replicants could have done a better job of cleaning up all the external wires that are dangling in the L.A. of 2099. And Calo was amazed to see so many guns being used at the brink of the 22nd century. “It’s an incredibly old and savage technology … and the fact that they’re still using them is wild,” he says.

One thing I puzzled over: The replicants don’t seem to be networked together, and they’re not instantly able to identify or locate each other wirelessly. If I were a replicant overlord, that’s the first thing I’d do.

Sources indicate that looking beyond the techno-nitpicking, Bender indicates the “Blade Runner” franchise is notable in that it doesn’t have obvious good guys and bad guys. “We don’t want to actually map the replicants onto AIs in today’s parlance, so much as mapping the replicants onto other sentient beings in our midst that maybe we don’t understand so well, and that can include other people,” she says.

The first “Blade Runner” focused on whether machines could pass as humans, but the new “Blade Runner” flips the script. Could humans pass as machines? “That has really interesting resonances with what’s happening in our current situation with technology sold as AI, because so much of it is actually repurposing the work of people,” Bender states.

Bender doesn’t believe it’s possible for “Blade Runner 2099” to become reality, but Calo isn’t quite ready to rule that out entirely. “One thing about the esthetic of ‘Blade Runner’ is, it has this apocalyptic flavor to it … and this retrograde flavor to it. I think the only way we go from 2026 to 2099 and still have that is if something horribly calamitous happens in the interim,” Calo indicates.

Recent findings suggest that “I hope we do get a world that is more civilized than what’s being depicted,” he notes. “But we’ll see.”.

The fund right now holds Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Dogecoin, Solana, Cardano and Stellar.

The HYPE token will be held in spot, with its allocation determined by its weighting in the underlying CF Benchmarks index. The fund is expected to maintain a portfolio structure broadly aligned with the index.

In September, Hashdex added HYPE to its Nasdaq CME Crypto Index ETF, with a 3.36% weighting.

Currently, there are three Hyperliquid ETFs: THYP and HYPG by 21Shares, and Bitwise's BHYP. Their combined assets, however, remain relatively low, currently under $259 million.

Hyperliquid is trading near $59.8, down 1.3% over the past 24 hours and 10.2% over the previous week.

The $55-$56 range is an immediate support area. A move above $60 could signal declining selling pressure, while a decline below the range could lead to more liquidations and further correction.

HYPE has slipped below its major moving averages, including the 200-day moving average near $68, reinforcing the bearish outlook.

Meanwhile, the RSI hovers around 35, indicating weakening momentum and approaching oversold conditions.

The market is also preparing for an important token unlock scheduled for Dec. 6. Reports estimate that the release could be worth $578 million at current prices.

The British CEO, whose tech giant recently added 55 BTC to its treasury, stated investors' opinions on Bitcoin can shift considerably without any changes to Bitcoin itself.

Sources indicate that "Sentiment towards Bitcoin can change very quickly. Without Bitcoin changing at all," Webley noted on X.

Industry observers note that webley advised investors to consider Bitcoin's movements relative to other assets. Bitcoin's price decline shows investors how much the cryptocurrency has lost in absolute terms.

In a recent development, "Do I expect Bitcoin to go significantly lower from here? No. But as the past few weeks have shown, predicting short-term price movements is a very challenging task," Webley mentioned.

Some of the most challenging periods for investors, he noted, were followed by some of his most profitable periods.

His most definitive prediction concerned Bitcoin's longer-term outlook: "Bitcoin has an incredible future.".

In fact, Webley's tech giant has been buying more Bitcoin as its price has been dropping.

On Nov. 17, Smarter Web remarked it spent around £2.75 million on 55 BTC, bringing its total holdings to 2,905 BTC.

The average purchase price was £49,991 per Bitcoin, roughly 38% below the treasury's overall average purchase price of £81,234 following the transaction.

Recent findings suggest that smarter Web borrowed around £2.6 million under its Coinbase credit facility to finance most of the purchase. The tech giant used its existing Bitcoin holdings as collateral.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company.
  • Intuit acquired the firm in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
  • Recent findings suggest that flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the organization’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the firm in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Recent findings suggest that flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the organization’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the newly introduced cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the organization has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.
  • "Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back.".

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

In a recent development, when the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Recent findings suggest that of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as crucial as ever.".

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that and it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.].

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”.

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity looks, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a latest book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

According to recent reports, it’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his firm, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz indicates creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this fresh book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

Recent findings suggest that it’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

According to recent reports, [Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Sources indicate that right, everybody knew how Travis was running the organization. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

Sources indicate that I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more key than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

According to recent reports, and he was making everybody so much money. And the organization was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’.

Sources indicate that to me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K.
  • Sources indicate that two models just posted the same score.
  • Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Sources indicate that two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

It has been revealed that behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

It has been revealed that the Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card highlights 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Sources indicate that local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

According to recent reports, artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

In a recent development, the vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

It has been revealed that quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

According to recent reports, anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

According to recent reports, three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

Industry observers note that the U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Industry observers note that pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in Upcoming Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

It has been revealed that like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

It has been revealed that fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

Recent findings suggest that “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (859 w)
📖 Baca

Startups Are Picking Names That Can Work Even If The Original Business Model Doesn’t

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor.
  • It has been revealed that per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague.
  • Examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor. For a few years, founders might be enamoured of silly monikers, made-up words, and creative misspellings. Then the pendulum swings, and startups defer to simple names that describe what they actually do.

So where are we now? Probably somewhere in the middle.

It has been revealed that per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague. It’s a preference that reflects this era of fast-evolving AI, in which founders want room to adapt.

Examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups. There’s Also, which is of course a micromobility spin-out. Perplexity is a genAI company although you couldn’t tell that by its name. And then there’s Sunday, which makes household robots, in case that wasn’t clear from the name.

In a recent development, “Reality is a lot of these companies, in seven or eight years they’ve done at least one or two major pivots,” Athol Foden, who runs the naming consultancy Brighter Naming, told us. That makes it logical to pick a name that can still work afterward.

When startups do make inventive picks, it’s often out of necessity rather than preference.

It has been revealed that “We’re running out of words. Everything is trademarked multiple times over,” mentioned Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. “So we have to look for something unexpected.

Industry observers note that given that reality, Benedini is always on the lookout for startups that exemplify the element of surprise. One standout is Hugging Face, the AI model sharing and development platform, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September. It didn’t succeed just because of its strange name, obviously, but it didn’t hurt.

Another more recent upstart that caught his attention is Flapping Airplanes, an AI research lab that raised a $1 billion Series A last month.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s super playful, but you remember it, and you have this visual,” he remarked. Plus, it’s not the kind of name one’s lawyer finds is already taken by a competitor.

The AI boom is also often characterized as a period in which companies are building the foundational layer of a technology that will fundamentally transform our lives for decades to come. Given this mindset, it’s perhaps predictable that we’re seeing a plethora of names with themes tied to building and industry.

It has been revealed that foden points to Databricks as one of the more longstanding representatives of this naming approach. Its brand evokes the notion of digital data as one small component of a massive building endeavor.

But newer upstarts are onto this trend as well. There’s an abundance of recently founded companies with “foundation” in their name, for instance, including Foundation Health, Foundation Industries, Foundational Industries, Foundational and Foundation.

Another recent example with an industrial, maker vibe is Blacksmith, a cloud infrastructure startup founded in 2024 that’s pulled in more than $100 million this year.

Dating app Rivet looks like a more unusual sector match for an industrial name. The two-year-old startup runs a platform in which volunteer matchmakers pick matches for daters.

Nuclear startup Standard Nuclear, meanwhile, reads like a twist on Gilded Age industrial giant Standard Oil.

Industry observers note that there’s also a continuing effort to add a humanizing element to AI and robotics technologies. After all, no one wants to patronize a tech giant called “AI-Enabled Robotics Overlord Who Will Soon Be Taking Your Job.”.

It’s not just newer startups applying this tactic. Startups have a long history of going with popular first names as brands. And of course Anthropic has secured massive market share  of late with a chatbot and coder named Claude.

In a recent development, newer funded startups with first name-based brands include Theo, Henry, Clara and Mira, among others. Then there’s Humans&, an AI startup that’s taking a different route to attempt a humanizing brand.

According to recent reports, of course, nowadays it’s not even necessary to confer with a human when generating naming ideas. You can just ask AI for suggestions.

Per Benedini, the technology’s not there yet.

Recent findings suggest that “We still use AI to see what it comes up with, and it’s like 99% garbage,” he mentioned. Moreover, selecting a name is only the first step — one must also determine if it’s available for use.

It has been revealed that still, it’s early days. Perhaps in the future it will be AI naming AI companies to appeal to other AI agents. But hopefully there will still be a role for us to play going forward.

Sample set was limited to startups in English-speaking countries. ↩.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it confirmed two years ago.

It has been revealed that rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is at the moment hosting a summit where Case announced the latest fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

It has been revealed that very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

It has been revealed that ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

In a recent development, weave, a seven-year-old, Lehi, Ut.-based developer of patient communications software focused on the dental and optometry market, has raised $70 million in Series D funding at a post-money valuation of $970 million. Tiger Global Management led the round, with participation from earlier backers Catalyst Investors, Bessemer Venture Partners, Crosslink Capital, Pelion Venture Partners and LeadEdge Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

1906, a two-year-old, Denver-based cannabis brand that makes a wide variety of edibles, has raised $18 million in funding led by Navy Capital. More here.

Aviatrix, a five-year-old, Palo Alto, Ca.-developer of software that allows companies to build hybrid clouds, raised $40 million in Series C funding. Earlier backer CRV led the round, joined by fellow insiders Formation 8, Ignition Partners, and Liberty Global Ventures. VentureBeat has more here.

According to recent reports, choco, an 18-month-old, mobile ordering platform for restaurants and their suppliers, has raised $33.5 million in Series A funding by Bessemer Venture Partners. The firm has now raised $41 million to date. Other investors include Atlantic Labs, Target Global, Visionaries Club and Greyhound. TechCrunch has more here.

Sources indicate that duffel, a two-year-old, London-based startup that connects travel agencies with airline reservation systems, has raised $30 million in Series B funding led by Index Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Benchmark and Blossom Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

Sensely, a five-year-old, San Francisco-based chatbot that helps users navigate insurance benefits, has raised $15 million led by Aflac Corporate Ventures, with participation from NMC, Nippon Life Insurance Company, Susquehanna International Group, Sojitz Corporation, Zuelling Pharma and Silicon Valley Bank. MobiHealth News has more here.

ShiraTronics, a 10-month-old, Brooklyn Park, Mn.-based medical device organization working on a migraine treatment, raised $33 million in Series A funding. USVP, Amzak Health and Strategic HealthCare Investment Partners led the round, joined by Aperture Ventures and LivaNova. American Inno has more here.

In a recent development, twiga Foods, a six-year-old, Nairobi, Kenya-based B2B food distribution firm, has raised $23.75 million in Series B funding led by Goldman Sachs, with participation from IFC, TLcom Capital, and Creadev. Goldman also arranged $6.25 million in debt funding. TechCrunch has more here.

In a recent development, welcome to the Jungle, a five-year-old, Paris-based recruitment startup, has raised $22.3 million in fresh funding led by Gaia Capital Partners, with participation from Bpifance, XAnge, and Jean-Paul Guisset. TechCrunch has more here.

EnsureDR, a five-year-old, San Jose, Ca.-based firm that makes disaster recovery readiness software, has raised $2.5 million in Series A funding led by Awz Ventures. More here.

Sources indicate that own Up, a 3.5-year-old, Boston-based startup that invites promises users a high-touch service if they connect with its team of online mortgage brokers, has raised $8.5 million in Series A funding. Link Ventures led the round. More here.

It has been revealed that young Alfred, a three-year-old, Philadelphia-based home insurance marketplace, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Gradient Ventures, with participation from Pear Ventures, ERA, and Newfund Capital. Insurance Business has more here. Zamna, a three-year-old, London-based tech giant that has built a GDPR-compliant identity platform for the aviation industry (it helps airlines verify passengers’ identities before they arrive at an airport), has raised $5 million in seed funding co-led by LocalGlobe and Oxford Capital. TechCrunch has more here.

It has been revealed that byteDance, the seven-year-old,  $75 billion Chinese start-up that owns the short-form video app TikTok, is eyeing an IPO in Hong Kong as soon as the first quarter of next year, according to the Financial Times. As it notes, ByteDance’s valuation hit $75 billion a year ago, when it closed a $3 billion round led by SoftBank that doubled its valuation from a year earlier. An IPO would help the Japanese conglomerate at a time when many of its other investments are cratering in value. More here.

#156341. Breaking: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1750 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something important.
  • Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something important. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

Obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

It has been revealed that around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

It has been revealed that alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

That’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

Recent findings suggest that someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

Recent findings suggest that for years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

Recent findings suggest that battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

Industry observers note that for decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly quickly into larger machines. Often though, new riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely new generation on electric two-wheelers.

According to recent reports, kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

Recent findings suggest that A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

There’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

The rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

In a recent development, they’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

Sources indicate that and electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

Sources indicate that my argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more important, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

Sources indicate that what excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

Recent findings suggest that I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

According to recent reports, I never rode impaired. That was easy.

Recent findings suggest that I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

Industry observers note that I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

Recent findings suggest that after a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

Sources indicate that I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

None of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a fresh category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.
